name: Compton Gamma Ray Observatory (STS-37)
payload: Gamma Ray Observatory: 34,527 lb (about 15,700 kg) at the arm, the heaviest payload the robotic arm had moved, with four instruments (BATSE, OSSE, COMPTEL, EGRET); crew of five
first: The Shuttle flight that released the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory from the robotic arm after a contingency spacewalk freed its stuck antenna
description: STS-37 launched Atlantis from pad 39B on 5 April 1991 at 14:22:45 UTC with the Gamma Ray Observatory, the second of NASA's four Great Observatories, in its payload bay. On flight day 3 the arm raised the observatory, but its high-gain antenna would not deploy, and shaking it with thrusters and with the arm failed. A contingency spacewalk by Jerry Ross and Jay Apt followed, and the antenna was freed early in it. The arm released the observatory at 22:36:47 UTC on 7 April, three revolutions late. A planned spacewalk on flight day 4 tested equipment and arm handling. Atlantis landed at Edwards Air Force Base on 11 April, a day late because of high winds. The observatory, later named Compton, worked until June 2000; NASA lists 4 June 2000 as its end, when it reentered the atmosphere.

events.label: ANTENNA STUCK
events.note: The high-gain antenna would not deploy; shaking it with thrusters and the arm failed, and a contingency spacewalk freed it. The report gives no clock time.

events.label: OBSERVATORY RELEASED
events.note: Released by the arm at 22:36:47 UTC on 7 April, three revolutions later than planned.

events.label: LANDING
events.note: Edwards lakebed runway 33, 11 April 1991, 13:55:29 UTC, a day late for high winds.
